cells.tense: You're here at the desk, pen in hand, steady rather than bracing.
cells.ask: Hand one small piece of the shape to someone else this week — an afternoon's worth — and at the end of that day write down what actually happened while you weren't holding it.
cells.core:
You hold the form and keep the fire going at the same time. The messy thing comes to you, you make it workable, then you keep people moving when stopping would be easier — and you probably don't notice you're doing it.

What's open to you now is appetite: a fresh look at a form you haven't tried, curiosity about what the thing wants to become. Not a demand, just the next place this steadiness can spend itself. The handoff is the test. Watch what holds without you in the room, and notice what you already built well enough to leave.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the thing going and you make it hold together — both at once.
cells.verb: keeping something going — holding the fire for others and yourself without burning out
cells.place: the part of a life where you put shape on things — making a form that can carry what's coming

cells.tense: You're already in next quarter, running the shape before anything has arrived to fill it.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you're most ahead on and write what's true about it today — the numbers, its actual state — no projections. Then choose one step from that page.
cells.core:
You're not just holding the form — you're pushing it forward before it's ready to go. You can see the version where it works, and you're trying to build that version now, in a present that hasn't agreed to it yet. The push buys a few months. Then the timing catches up and the thing you were carrying starts carrying you.

When direction comes from what you actually feel about the thing, instead of what you've already decided it needs to become, the whole job gets lighter. The test is small: what's true right now, before the projection? Write that down and act from it. Nothing here says stop caring about next year — just let next year arrive at its own speed so what you're building stays yours.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding the shape ahead of the thing that needs it.
cells.verb: keeping something going — holding the fire for others and yourself without burning out

cells.tense: You're at a door that already closed behind you, still deciding whether to knock.
cells.ask: Write down the smallest thing you've been meaning to structure and leave it where you'll see it tomorrow — just the putting down, no sorting yet.
cells.core:
The shape you used to make isn't coming right now. Something you wanted to hold together has gone quiet, and pressing on it doesn't work — effort against the quiet just wears you down. That's the honest part. Effort isn't the tool here.

What this is for is releasing what's finished so the next thing has room — letting the old form end without filing it as a failure. Back in balance, direction comes from what you actually feel, not from what you think you still owe. One small structure, put down where tomorrow's eyes will find it, is enough to start the pull.

cells.tense: You're already writing the shape — pen down, calling it the room's.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you set up in the last week and say out loud to yourself, once, 'I made that.' That's the whole ask.
cells.core:
Look at the last week honestly. Something you set up is running — a schedule, a check-in, a way of doing the thing — and you'd probably say it just happened that way, or the group sorted it, or it was obvious. It wasn't obvious. You made a call about what should hold and you put it in place.

The shape is running and you haven't stood beside it. Nothing's wrong; this is the work doing itself without your name on it. The return is smaller than you'd think: say the making once, to yourself, in plain words. The next one is easier to own.

attempts.check: The record gives me the card's behavior (sustained motivation, tending a fire, inspiring others to keep going), the seat's function (making a form that holds complexity), and each medicine's specific action. It does not give me any single person's history, so the cores stay on the mechanism and never claim to know why someone is where they are. A reader could reasonably say 'tending the fire' is not everyone's version of drive in a structured role, so the cells describe the shape in plain words — holding the thing up, keeping it going — and leave the reader room to disagree. The asks are one physical act each (write it down, say the number out loud, keep one promise at the size it was made), so they still teach the person something even if my read is off. The sentence that serves me most is 'Tending the fire doesn't need an audience' — it sounds good and does work the person did not ask for; it goes.
